title: Amritsar Police Bust Pakistan-Linked Terror Module, Seize AK-47 and Grenades
excerpt: Amritsar Rural Police arrested 28-year-old truck driver Navjot Singh and recovered an AK-47 rifle, two hand grenades and nine live cartridges allegedly pushed across the border by drone.
body:
• Amritsar Rural Police on Sunday busted a Pakistan-linked terror module, arresting 28-year-old truck driver Navjot Singh and recovering an AK-47 rifle with a magazine and nine live cartridges, two hand grenades, a mobile phone and a motorcycle.
  • Inspector General of Police (Border Range) Gurpreet Singh Bhullar said the weapons had been pushed into Indian territory by drones and were linked to a Pakistan-based ISI handler and a second handler in the Middle East. The accused had been promised Rs 50,000 but had received no money before his arrest.
  • This is the third AK-47 recovered by Amritsar Rural Police. A case has been registered under the Arms Act and the Explosive Substances Act at the Gharinda police station, and investigators are working to establish the network's forward and backward linkages.
  • People in Punjab's border districts who spot unidentified drones or dropped parcels should alert the police or BSF rather than touching them — anti-drone teams and cordon-and-search operations are running along the border, the IGP said.

AMRITSAR: Amritsar Rural Police on Sunday dismantled a cross-border arms and explosives supply network with the arrest of a 28-year-old man and the recovery of an AK-47 assault rifle, two live hand grenades and ammunition — a haul police said could have been used in a major terror or criminal strike.

Director General of Police (DGP) Punjab Gaurav Yadav announced the breakthrough, saying the accused had been intercepted while riding a motorcycle and was found carrying an AK-47 rifle with a magazine and nine live cartridges, two hand grenades, a mobile phone and the motorcycle itself. The arrested man has been identified as Navjot Singh, alias Cheema, a 28-year-old truck driver and resident of Sarai Manthan Khan in the Tarn Taran district.

The operation

Inspector General of Police (Border Range) Gurpreet Singh Bhullar told a press conference that the operation was carried out on precise intelligence inputs by special teams of the Amritsar Rural Police led by Senior Superintendent of Police Kanwalpreet Singh Chahal, with SP (D) Ramanvinder Singh, DSP Yadavinder Singh of Attari and CIA Inspector Manmeet Singh on the ground.

https://x.com/ANI/status/2106691163696824603

Bhullar said this was the third AK-47 recovered by the Amritsar Rural Police, and called the hand grenades particularly concerning because of the large-scale loss of life such explosives can cause. He termed the seizure a major preventive success, saying the recovery had potentially stopped the material from being used in a serious crime. The team behind the operation will be recommended for awards and honours before the DGP and the Chief Minister.

The cross-border trail

According to police, the weapons had been pushed into Indian territory through drones by handlers linked to Pakistan's ISI and smugglers operating from abroad. Preliminary investigation revealed links to a Pakistan-based ISI handler and another handler in the Middle East, Bhullar said.

Police said Navjot Singh was a drug user who had previously been involved in cross-border heroin and drug trafficking. This time, the foreign handlers assigned him a different consignment: deliver the weapons to an unknown contact — a "cut-out" — at a location in a neighbouring district, with further instructions to follow. The handlers concealed their identities using virtual numbers and the cut-out system so no link in the chain knew the others. The accused had been promised up to Rs 50,000 but had received no money before his arrest.

A case has been registered on the complaint of the CIA wing at the Gharinda police station, and an intensive investigation is under way to uncover the full network, trace the origins of the seized weapons and identify their intended recipients. Bhullar said the exact target could not be disclosed at this stage.

A familiar pattern on the border

The bust fits a pattern Punjab Police have warned about for months: weapons and explosives delivered by drone across the international border, routed through criminal networks that move between drug smuggling and arms trafficking. The IGP said security had been tightened in coordination with the Border Security Force (BSF), with a second line of defence, dedicated anti-drone teams and continuous cordon-and-search operations in the border belt. The operation was conducted under the Punjab government's stated zero-tolerance policy against organised crime, gangsters and terrorism.

What's next

The accused is being questioned intensively to map the network's contacts and the technical aspects of the drone drops. Intelligence agencies have been informed, and police said further arrests were likely as the forward and backward linkages are established. For the large Punjabi diaspora in Canada, the US and the UK — many of whose families still live in the Tarn Taran-Amritsar belt — the bust is another reminder of how closely Punjab's border security is tied to everyday safety in the frontier districts.
